items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I was engaged by Andy Kirk to replace a trumpeter named Clarence Trice... I stayed with the orchestra for four months

ctx.x: When I joined Benny, the only musicians that I knew well were Shad Collins, Russell Smith, Sandy Williams and Milt Robinson. The rest had come to the scene while I was tooting in Europe. But I soon became well acquainted with the others and Ulysses Livington lived not far from me at 155th Street and St. Nicholas Avenue, so we became very good friends.

Benny's band was great to work for. He would get close to his musicians, talk with them, and go out drinking with them. The fact that he could really converse with them and that he also knew how to put a band together meant that in many ways his bands were excellent. He could take a band, and in two weeks you would think that the guys had been playing together forever. Besides being a clever arranger, he also knew how to explain what he wanted. The only problem with his bands was that they somehow never seemed to…

There was a bar called "Fat Mans" just under where Ulysses lived. Fat Mans' was Charles Turner and he played bass in Marion Hardy's Alabamians, the band that Cab Calloway came to New York with, and whom I played opposite at the Savoy with Scott. Fat Man and Eddie Mallory, a trumpet player with Hardy's band, had opened the bar together, but Fat Man eventually bought out Eddie's interest and was the sole owner. It was a very modern bar and became quite a hangout for musicians that mostly lived in the neighbourhood.

items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Ram, George Johnson, Buster and myself were with Burton.

ctx.x: Kirby had a contract at Burton's for only one month, so when our time was up, he had not received another contract but promised us that he would have work for us in a few days because his agent was working on a deal. It came through - Kirby told us that the band had a gig in some town about fifty miles from Oakland.

But Bill Beason had gone back to New York without saying anything to anyone or giving Kirby a notice. However, Kirby found a guy to replace Beason and we left for the gig in two rented cars. Kirby drove one and Burton the other (Burton had arranged the gig). Kirby had the instruments in the car he was driving and the drummer. Ram, George Johnson, Buster and myself were with Burton.

Burton wore very thick glasses and as we were going to the gig, he told us that he had been drafted in the Army but was discharged because of his eyesight was bad and one night, he had driven a truck into one of the barracks on the Army post. It was beginning to get dark and we noticed that whenever a car was coming at us from the opposite direction, Burton would slow down from the 45 miles an hour he was doing. I began to believe Burton's story about his discharge from the Army and didn't feel too secure with him.
